Web crawling is designed to facilitate discovery of URLs, which contrasts from web scraping in which data is extracted from websites; examples of common web crawlers include Google Search and Microsoft Bing.14,15 In our study, URLs were gathered via web crawling in effort to study relationships between websites and did not include the extraction of copyrighted material. Major web crawlers follow certain policies, one of which is a politeness policy that outlines how to avoid overloading websites and includes elements such as the robots exclusion standard.16 The robots exclusion standard is a communication standard proposed by Martijn Koster in 1994 which enables websites to specify which areas of the site web crawlers may or may not access as well as designate a minimum interval between visits (the specific visit interval required by a website can be found in the crawl-delay section of the website’s robots.txt file).17 This standard, which has been discussed within the literature, enables web crawlers to adhere both to content ethicality (the practice of adhering to appropriate sections of a website) and access ethicality (compliance with designated visit intervals in order to preserve site performance).17 All major search engine bots, or web crawlers, conform to the robots exclusion standard and will therefore read and obey the instructions given by the robots.txt file.18,19 In addition, the Sitemaps protocol was introduced by Google in 2005 to inform search engines about URLs contained in a website which are available for web crawlers to access.20,21 This protocol allows web crawlers to more efficiently access and find URLs on a website. It was created as a complement to the robots exclusion protocol and has since been publicly supported by Microsoft, Yahoo!, IBM and multiple U.S. state government websites including Arizona, California, Utah and Virginia.22,23 The database created in this study contained each of the top-level URLs associated with each web page in our academic medical center dataset. For example, a top-level domain, corresponding to a website’s homepage, may contain the URL: www.universityhospital.org. A subdomain, or internal link, of this web page may contain information regarding team members and be associated with the URL: www.universityhospital.org/team. Other subdomains may also include topics such as care services provided, and location. Included in this data extraction were internal links, inlinks and outlinks. Table 2 contains definitions of these terms. The internal links (i.e. subdomains) served as nodes, or endpoints in the network analysis. Inlinks are links between web pages on a single website: these serve as internal edges, or links that connect nodes inside the subgraph being analyzed. Outlinks serve as external edges, or links between nodes that are inside the subgraph and those outside. Table 2. Network topology terminology and definitions.
